The job is when they get off from work, some of them wouldn't go home until the time to come back to work the next night and all that kind of stuff. Nobody never walked or rode home. See they used to have dance halls up and down, and they'd all meet at the E-light on Ramport Street in the morning. You know what I'm saying? And they'd walk up all the barrooms, all the way uptown, you know, for Andrew Anderson, he was one of them. Yeah. Or Foster's cousin.
And they would walk, they would never ride uptown.
No, you see, because we'd walk, you see, because we'd go in them places and everybody knew them, they had credit accounts and bad liquor, you know, that spook down.
You could throw all the bars before you get home? Huh?

Might take a whole day to get home, you could throw all those bars. You could throw all these, you could throw them in there. And they went ahead and join that, you understand? And then we went back down to the entertainers downtown there, where Russ had, he used to put us in jail every Monday. Every Monday? Every Monday. And get right out. Why did he do that? Why did they put you in jail? I don't know. We just picked us up, raved the place. How long did you stay in jail? Until they called our name and we come right out. I see we was up there in Carlton playing one night, with Handy's job, with Law & Quarter. And all we were playing down handy, we got half loaded and was playing down and we started shooting in the hand and got shot in the foot or something like that. And they put us all in jail. And we went up there and brought them to the hospital and said, where was you when the shooting started? And I said, I don't want to play in jail. Well there used to be another guy who used to play up a lot of trumpets. He'd come down there with Handy and what's he called, he used to play all that trumpet like Lewis Armstrong.
Was he better than Guy Kelly?

That's the one I'm talking about, Guy Kelly. Yeah, Guy, you understand? And Guy, we was at Chinatown one night and South Stand was at the Bulls out there. You understand? So Guy, a good friend of mine said, Guy, I hate this.

We were talking. We were talking. We were talking. We were talking. We were talking before about Guy Kelly and South Stand being with the Bulls. Oh yeah. Guy Kelly. Yeah. That's the story about it. What happened? Yeah.

Well, he was playing with the Bulls out there. And around one o'clock just before they closed up time, Guy Kelly, they played fireworks, you know, it's an introduction, something like that. You understand? That's why Guy come on like that. And what I mean, we was, Kuyper had shot a number at him, stomping at the Savoy, you know? And Guy come back with that. And right after that night he went to Chicago with, started playing Three Deucers down in State Street. He was down there with Art Tatum and this guy, da you know, composed that saxophone that got killed in an automobile right there.
Chewberry?
Chewberry, yeah.
Composed Christopher Columbus. Yeah. You went up to Chicago, you must have been to Chicago too since you know the streets and everything.
Oh I lived in Chicago. Oh you did? But I wasn't playing music, you understand. I didn't learn how to play music until I come back, yeah.
Well how old were you when you came back?
Well I was, just had put on long pants, I was a young boy. You must have been about sixteen.
Seventeen, yeah.
Sixteen, yeah.
When you came back, did you leave the Chicago?

Well I didn't start to get together with the banjo until I was about nineteen, yeah so nineteen or twenty. Yeah. You see that's when I started. You see I was playing that youth, swung from the youth to tenor banjo.
Then you lived in New Orleans from then on?

Yeah. Outside of the times when we was on the road, you know, going different places. Did you go on the road a lot? Oh yeah, when you see them bands, we used to give them gigs all through Louisiana, Texas, and different places like that. You know. And I was out there with Ike Garnett, with a group in Crowley, they're called the Yelping Hounds, I was out there with a group out there, and Victor De Spencer at the Shadowland, Victor De Spencer got the Shadowland. Well he had a band, he had a band too, with old man John Porter playing and Blake playing drums and Bunk was on trumpet and a boy by the name of, from St. Martinville, no he was from Lafayette, Edgar Mouton, he was playing sax, or you know Bunk was playing trumpet, you remember Bunk? And this guy, Hampton, playing trombone. Must have been years ago. Yeah, well I mean, and we had Tank Baptiste playing piano. Yeah. You see, but I was a youngster playing with older men than I was. And we had a council from Brobridge who used to play, he was automobile mechanic, played saxophone. You see, that was the New Orleans Cotton Club band, the Krells used to call it the New Orleans Coddy Pequon, you understand, and old man, and we had Al Agretta playing piano with us. Yeah, you heard of him, Al Agretta, he's in California now teaching and something like that. He was a great piano player. We had a good band.
Was this the Yelping Hounds you're talking about?
No, this was Cotton Club, Victor Spencer. Victor Spencer.
Had the Yelping Hounds.

No, he had this band. Yelping Hounds, see Crowley was our Louisiana, with the exception of the year, jump off, you know. You see when we were hitting Lake Charles and all them different places, we'd take it from Crowley all the way, the Orange and all them places.
Yeah. Well I didn't understand what happened to Celestan when Guy Kelly and Kuyper were there.
Well Kuyper, I never remember Kuyper was with a- At the Bulls Club you're talking about? Oh yeah, at the Bulls Club.
What happened to Celestan? He sat in the corner and held his own?

No, well at that time Guy, Campbell and Miss Janet and all of them was playing with Celestan then. Yeah. But I was back there at Chinatown, raising the devil with them boys, you see. We had a guy that was added attraction to that band, you understand, and after he left. See Celestan, anybody come, Sue was buried high, I mean Cindy Desvene too, you know. They were high, frankly all out of town. Now Cindy had a band, Bucket from Chicago and Porter was from Detroit and they had a lot of boys from Natchez and different places. And there was another trumpet player, Eugene Ware and all that bunch, they was with the bands. And then Joe Robichaux started scalping, him and Kill Dee they just started scalping, going around there getting men out of this band, that band, made him up a band when he was back there at the Rhythm Club. Russ went back there with him for a while, you understand. But of course Russ was a better bass or a drum player, he was kind of weak but he just was a good friend of mine, I just let him have it. You know, then I started, I had Manuel Cruz still playing with me at one time, and a different guy. Gilbert Young used to play too with him.
Well who was in the Yelping Hounds? I never remember.

I'd gone and he was the manager of the Yelping Hounds, he was a tennis action phone player. And Buster Meehy, well they was booting his buddies out of Texas, out of Houston, well they left there and come on back and phoned up a band around there. And then they had another little ordinary band, Sun Shields, he had a little get together, out there around there too. Well there's two little minor bands and I know you heard talk of those guys who used to play so much trumpet, they, let's see what, he got, Kilt used to call them high notes trumpet player out there. He got Kilt in the Rain, he used to play with us too, I can't think of his name right now. Oh, E. Van Thomas? Thomas, E. Van Thomas? He got Kilt in the Rain. He got Kilt in the Rain. He had a brother, by the name of Willie, used to play with drumsticks, with chair rounds for drumsticks, Willie's brother, the one who got killed playing trumpet, but I can't call him.
Is he the one that got killed by this convict? Yeah, E. Van Thomas. E. Van, that's it.
Yeah, E. Van. Yeah, E. Van. Yeah, in Crowley, yeah. How did he get killed?
Hmm? How did he get killed? Convict. Convict.

You see the people in Rain, Louisiana, that's seven miles from Crowley. Practically everybody in that town is related to each other. You understand what I mean? I mean they distance cousins. It's a very small town.
Yeah, it was a very small town.

And Buster Millier was a guy that looked like Gilbert Young, but he played like Sun Johnson. And his daddy used to be the pool walker at the Crowley Social Hall, and he'd come around there that night and all we could do was tell us not to go there. You see we used to go there and get liquor, you know, that used to handle that sheriffs and things, they used to handle all that bad liquor. You understand? And we left there and a couple of days after that we had a date in Church Point. We played a wedding out there, a white wedding, and it was reminding you of the cowboy days. We had to stay a bond about three days. It was a feudal between two families, one didn't want the other to marry the other, and it was like on the right we were all out that way. And we left there and we went on to El Lerato, Arkansas. And we left El Lerato and we went to McGee, Arkansas, we was crossing the street still. The red lights was down in the ground and we crossed the street. And the crankcase, I was with Victor Spencer then, we crossed the crankcase and tore the muffler or something under the car there, oil was leaking. So they put the whole band in jail, you understand? And so they put the whole band in jail there after we got there. And the sheriff said, with a big old ten gallon hat, say, I want you to teach this little girl how to play that fiddle. She had a ukulele. You understand? So I said, well she needs some books to learn how to play that instrument. I said, wait till the music store will open up tomorrow, we'll go down to town and see if I can. So I went down there and got some little books, you know where you put your finger on the ukulele, ain't going to rain no more, ain't going to rain no more, you understand? So the man said, you got to teach you how to play. So Gordy said, how? He said, that's what you get for being a band in jail prayer. Now they going to keep you here. No, now you going to stay here. I said, damn, that's all right, I ain't going to stay here soon. I said, oh yeah, you'll be here a long time until that little girl learned how to play that fiddle. So they kept us there, three or four days, and Judge Farnas said, how much y'all charge to play a dance? A hundred and seventy-five dollars. I said, that's what we're going to find in the audience. A hundred and seventy-five dollars. So we've been just laughing at me. So the little girl's mother said, well, they seem to be a nice bunch of guys. So they gave me twenty dollars for teaching the little girl. So they wanted something. I said, oh no, I was the guy that was going to stay here. You don't get a horn in on this.
But you didn't tell me what happened to Evanne.

Oh, Evanne was playing, you see. You weren't with him that time? No, I was in Crowley. You were close by, huh? Seven miles from there. Yeah. And Evanne was with some woman by the name of Mabel or something, this particular woman's husband had been in penitentiary, and the same day he got out of penitentiary, you understand me, he'd come up on the bandstand and joked him. But old man Ney, his son used to play like Son Johnson but he looked like Gilbert Young. Well he came around that because he used to.

like me telling me don't go over there, because a man woke up in his sleep and told us don't go over there, but God, I think a lot of them was over there, but I don't know, but I didn't go, you understand?
Well this was the floor walker telling you not to go.
Yeah, oh he was a barber too. He was a town barber and he had a son played in his, but what he liked me, because his son Buster thought so much of me, you know, like me.
But being the floor walker he'd know who was talking every time.

But he wasn't a floor walker of rain, he lived in the crowd. But he got up just like around the corner and come around here and tell me, say don't go over there tonight, because this particular guy that committed the crime just had got out of jail and knew that, see, Evanne, daddy was one of them old old doctors. He had a lot of little funny houses painted, white trim with blue and it looked like he took blue and made it to blue, you understand? And Evanne had a really nice place. He had went to Tuskegee, he was highly educated. He went to Tuskegee to learn how to, he was a tailor, you understand? He was a little dog father, he played up some trumpet, he was a high note man, you understand what I mean? And those people used to go for musicians then. See all them bands from Baton Rouge and stuff used to come through there, Dimes and all those bands used to come through those places. Well it would be that, see we'd get our kicks. Now this band with Victor Spencer, what I was in, they had Bunk playing trumpet, they had Bunk playing trumpet, Icy was playing bass, and this boy I told you a while ago was playing piano, Al Greta. And Blake used to be with the Sonny South band, he was from here.
Blake, Blake who?
Blake, Blake was his name.
Blake.
What did he play?
Drums.

What's his first name? I can't remember, he used to have a Sonny South band down there. And he was with- He was the manager of the band or the leader of the band? No. Victor Spencer was the manager of the band. The man got to Shadowland, his son got out there. But Gordette wrote for me to come, told me about they had so many gigs.
He's got the Shadowland where?
Out there on Dan Hill and Washington. Oh that one.
Yeah.
That's his son.
But anyway, how did this guy kill? He juged- Raised or something, knife or something like that.
He killed his staff?
Yeah. On the bandstand? Yeah, on the bandstand.
Oh yeah?
He just ran up there and killed him. You've heard about that, huh? Yeah, I heard he got killed, I didn't know. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, right over to Joyce Lewis.
I think his name was Gilbert.
He pushed Joyce Lewis in front of me. Should have pushed Father Al in front of me. You see the thing over there? You see, now a lot of stuff that you find out to do, you didn't know.

Yeah, that's right. Yeah. You see? Because I was in that section with those outfits. Did you play with them too? And they had Al, Booker's cousin Al, Al of Washington, Al, he died in Chicago, used to play tenor. Al was playing tenor with us out there.
Who was Booker?

Booker Washington used to play bass. He died. Oh yeah. Yeah, well that was his cousin. And they had another one, what they call, he's living back there kind of off now, Willie Washington, that's Booker's brother. He's back on Gileser Street out collecting insurance from him, you understand? Does he play music? Well he don't, having Joe Bentley and all that bunch used to play with Nat Tolles, you understand? Really? What they wanted to play with? They used to play out of Nat Tolles, Nat Tolles band, headquarters in the south was Monroe, but his headquarters was Nebraska Army Hall. And they had this little guy who used to play all that tenor. But him and Sam Dutry was a good friend. He's a radio technician now, what's his name? He played all that saxophone, big tone, big tone like Uskin Hawkeye, I can't think, there's so many of them guys, man. He lives here now? I don't know where he lives there. He could be, you know, he might be out there where Sam Dutry come, with his last wife Sam Dutry head out there.
Well anyway, who did you hear in Chicago when you were out there? Did you hear any music? Yeah.

I used to be out there, 28 in the league, out there, and Louis and them would be out there. Louis was living on, he was playing at the, you see, when Louis come up there, they sent for Lee Collins. You know they sent for René. And René didn't want to go, and Louis went. He was playing at the Royal Garden with Joe Oliver. You understand? You went there? No, I was a little bit too young. You understand what I mean? Well I was in Chicago when they come up there, you see. And I was living on East 36th Street with my uncle, you know what I'm saying? And that's the time I was going to, Al C. Boyd, well he was a cellar player, he used to be up in the old university where I attended school. You understand what I mean?
You were taking music lessons while you were out there too?

No, I didn't know how to play nothing. But I used to hear all the music singing all around Lake Michigan out there, you know, around the swimming hole and things. I'd go down to Grand Park down in Chicago and different things like that.
35thman State? Did you hang around 35thman?

Well, 30th way from State, well there was nothing at 33rd, 33rd in Indiana, that's where Grand Terrace was, you understand what I mean. Oral Hines was, or when he'd come up, I mean in these late years, well I mean I was down there then when Oral Hines was.
But around 35th and State were you around that area?

I used to go around there and slip in the pool room and shoot proof or something like that, you understand what I mean? But you couldn't get in there? No, no, there wasn't no music around there. You see, it was 30, 40th and Cottage Grove, that's where Joe Oliver was playing. And Miss Lil was playing piano with Joe Oliver and Louis got in the band and she was a graduate of Wilberforce and she got in with Louis and taught Louis how to read, you know, how to read music and things like that. And after Louis started reading music then he started recording for Decca and different things like that, you know, Decca, record recording.
When you came back to New Orleans, you didn't start playing music right away? No, I learned how to play ukulele. Did you used to go around and listen to bands here? No. You must have been about 19.

You see, my sister used to work for Nashville, Albany and St. Charles, she worked for the family of Wilberforce had the music store. And Franklin Burr, he was singing then, the man he called Perry Mason. You understand what I mean? And he was singing, he used to sing that on records. And she used to bring all them records home and things like that. And she started bringing a lot of records home, and I ain't got nobody, you know Bobby himself playing piano and stuff like that. He come from Pittsburgh and he got into Chicago and Louis formed up a band and branched off from Oliver and formed up his own band where he got Earl Hines. Earl Hines in Admiral's style, where he got all them the menaces and things that Louis was making. He knew music. See James P. Johnson taught Earl Hines and he taught, James P. Johnson taught Vatwiler too, yeah. Vatwiler was a piano player, but James P. Johnson and those fellas, he had Liotta Lyon, but Liotta Lyon he never did want to learn the music. He used to play all that close harmony. You understand what I mean? He'd smoke them big cigars and things like that. And old P. Johnson would be there now he could make you laugh. P. Johnson went down there in the village and he said I'm going to dedicate this number to a little Creole boy from there. Oh you know him? You married him too? Liotta Lyon?
Yeah.

Liotta Lyon was down there, or recorded with Al Hood when he was on this, what you call him here, Liotta Lyon. He, when you were going all over like I was, it was nice to meet everybody. You see, those bands like Jimmy Noon and all of them, they were coming down in northern part of Louisiana before they started coming here. You understand? You see all them bands used to come down there. See because everybody would turn out, you know it's like the Saints football game, everybody would turn out with all those bands. You understand? And there used to be some bad boys around there. You see, at the last, I was, when I was swimming with that thing every night, you see, things just come to me. I swooned at a banjo and stuff every night. And of course what I did today ain't nothing to what I can do. Maybe you might not believe me, or what the man's swimming, but you know you get rusty when you don't fool with them. You understand? You're like anything else. Or Tatum, and all that fun. Well, you see, after I learned how to play, and I wanted to see those guys, you understand? And pick up on their songs just like a guy, Duke Ellison and some of them come in town, well, they would have. It's like Dream, but he don't use no Apple Fire on his guitar. He's got a, what's he called, made that guitar for him. He used to take the certain type of wood that they would use to make the Freddie Green with Connelly and all of them. And I was a standby band, or rather Sidney Keith's band was a standby band, but Sidney couldn't play as much as me. And I got in there and played Serena and a couple of things like that and all those things. You see, it's just like a lift, it's like you get a lift with liquor when you ride them Greek guys. You see, they don't have jam sessions now like they used to. Before we moved from that Union Hall down there on Columbus and Playboy, it was a regular music conservatory. You could go down there and learn things, because they had guys there from everywhere playing up everything in there. You know what I mean? And the faster you get tired they would put another one on there. You know what I mean? White and color would be in there. And I mean there was so many things you could learn. You know what I'm saying? And I happened to be around some good sessions sometimes and I picked up on a lot of things. Now just like we was back there at Claiborne, I mean St. Bernard and Galvary, and I was playing back there with who? I was playing back there with a group, probably with Bud Banks and them I was playing back there with I'm not sure. And Danny Barker coming there. You understand? No I was back there with Sheik, that's right. I was back there with Cheik. Yeah I was going to ask you about that.
You did play with Cheik because Henry Russ told me about that.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. I was back there with Cheik and Danny Barker coming in. Who was in that band when you were working with Cheik?
You were working with Cheik in the 50's sometime, huh?
Yeah, we was working back at, we was working back on Roachie Bridge in London Avenue. And Henry Russ was playing bass out with you, wasn't he?
Yeah I believe he was.

We was back there with a group and they had a hole in the head, Walter, that boy we used to be with Fat Domino, his daddy. You know Walter. Yeah, Papoosh. Papoosh used to, Daddy used to be across the street. And Henry was down there with his brothers, never did get along with them brothers. You understand what I mean? That bass player and that guitar player, that Henry never could get along with them, that's why he never played with them. You understand what I mean? All that bunch was down there. I was down there with Cheik and this bunch.
I've been with the boys all right.
You understand? And we'd be down there riffing and playing all that kind of stuff. We had all the mumber up. We had the crowd, we'd do all the crowd down there where we was.
You had all those mumber on?

It used to be like a patio. We'd be playing that. They was playing like closed-end joints. You know what I'm saying? But they used to come down there with Cheik and da da Sheik. You played a lot with Cheik? I played a good bit with Cheik. You played guitar did it?
Yeah.
I played guitar with Cheik. But Howard too. You never played at Non-Preservation Hall down there? Where's that?
Preservation Hall in the past quarter?
No, I didn't. Once I played down at one carnival I'd be, no I ain't never played.

Well they've got a lot of good guys around there that's playing music, I can't think of them right now, that ain't never played down there. That's why they're down there borrowing money on the next job and all that kind of stuff. You see I'd rather do something if it was a quarter. I'd rather work and make me honest. You understand I mean music is a art. And you see like when I was playing music and things way back then, fellas like Sheep used to carry them people's instruments, who used to play with her, they never played in no band with me. You understand what I mean? You might think I'm lying. You understand that? Sheep never could be, he's chops gone or something like that. Now you take Albert Alcone, his chops is about gone but he's got a son that tells me it's pretty good. You understand what I mean? And that's why I just did something else. Because guys making all them bad notes, you see them fellas I come up with, you make a bad one, they tell you keep on making bad ones until you make a good one. Don't continue making the same bad one all the time.
That's what you think is the problem with the musicians today, they keep making the same bad ones. Or maybe they don't know the same. At least make another bad one or make the same bad ones.

I'm not going to say, listen, listen, go there, say, you and I are friends. I say, yeah. He say, you want to do me a favor? I say, what? He say, fire my son. You understand? Fire his own son out the band. Yeah, man. He fired his son.
Fireed him out my band, yeah.

He went with Joe Rose, so he was going to play a right, you understand that? Yeah. I just say my boy Danny worked with Kev, he must have carried the instruments himself. He's got to get all that, he's tuned up, got the artificial tuning on, if you understand what I mean. Of course I can play it, but I meant to say he's a nice brother and everything like that, but you see that kind of fellas like that used to play house parties around you, you know like somebody did a fish ride or piano band or something like that. Them fellas, man, you wouldn't go around there and call yourself playing no music. You see, a lot of them guys like Howard and them, I never would play with them, because Howard was a self-taught musician. He was a very persistent, he, in a way of speaking, he had drums, he swung from drums to trumpet. But them guys would get a deposit on the job and do away with all the money. What I mean the money in advance, they would do away with all the money when it was time to come up with a job, they had to get sample anybody. You understand? That type of guy would be glad to play with them. You understand what I mean? You understand? But like black and blue, or like this, when we cut off the stem of the play, why make me so black and blue and all them kind of numbers like that, you see, that's why it would help to kill poor Howard, because he had to blow himself to death to try to cover up, you know, all them rotten pension guys drawing pension, what he had in the band, but that's not the, but he did away with the money, you understand? He would have to go get that type of people. He had to get away with the can. Yeah, you feel it? Sad as McKellar's film, you understand? I mean, them guys couldn't do nothing. You understand me? So that's why, I got me at a gig, working or something like that, I said, if this beats a blank, I don't know why it would make me shame, you understand? I don't know. That's true. Yeah. But I asked the facts. Some of them is dead and gone, but God forgive me if I'm lying, that's the truth.
Who were the musicians that you really enjoyed playing and you think were really good?

Well, musicians I enjoyed playing with like Russ, Willie Humphrey, now Willie Humphrey come back here. They come back here and if you want to use a stick, I said, no, don't worry about the planet and get on the alto. So he got on the alto and started working that. I said, we got two of them. I said, we're going back there to St. Monica's, they got all them hells back there but we're going to give them religion tonight when we go back there. And the number when I played back there, just said come out, just before intermission we played it, Slow Boat to China. You understand me? That number just said come out, Slow Boat to China. We played that number. We swung this other number, Stomp at the Savoy. We swung that and then we swung the sunny side of the street. That's where Lionel's Crip. And then we swung that and then we swung the sunny side of the street. That's where Lionel's Crip. And Benny sounded like Art Tatum at times and Earl Hines. Benny. Benny Allen, he was big, he was Keeto's cousin. He lived in a great time. He died. Oh man he could play some bouncing. Oh talk about the piano. And Jerry Green, well Jerry Green had been with Clyde Carr and Houston with them big old Lion bands you know, he'd come over there with us with that bass and I had, he'd come over there with us and I had, he'd come over there with us and I had, he'd come over there with them, you know straighten them licks shorter on the bass and pray a bass and don't make a gang of noise, you understand what I mean? Play smooth. You see all that staccato, that wasn't easy, we need that legato, the smoothness, you understand what I mean? And that's where we went, that's where we stole the show with them people. Them people said, all them raggedy drummers, musicians, they can't play out all them guys, all dressed up, looking like Clark Gable. Yeah. Homie G was back there with that bass. He was with Henry Horton. Listen, all this stuff I'll tell you about, open confession is good for the soul, they'll tell you. Poor Jew and Garth, but we give religion, all the bad boys. I don't know if Garth must have got his lips fired down that night because he was a good musician too. He was piano playing and everything. Did you ever meet him? Never. I never met him twice. Yeah, Gladys.
Yeah, well all them boys.

I had some bad boys playing with me. I had some bad boys playing with me. And well that's right, all of them could play. I wouldn't hide nobody. See, Carl and them, they wanted to be the outstanding guy. I didn't care how much you played, as long as you played right. You understand what I mean? Of course now people like in these late years like George Lewis and them, well they come about like cuckoos and that bunch come about. Well the times that I'm telling you about these fellas, they was good musicians in their time but they couldn't touch it. Like Hugh Albert and all that, he got trouble with the Tawana bass, that ain't nothing but like them old time guys, ta They used to play that a long time ago, yeah.
Was George Lewis old fashioned and good boy with that old time in him?

Yeah, he was old fashioned. And you see like this boy played with Thomas would play with Celestan. All that, he was more modern than all of them because he couldn't read but he was nice coming up, but all of them, they come back and shawky, Banana brought back that. René used to teach shawky, you understand, you didn't know that did you?
No.

Yeah. John Porter was the bass player. With who? With Risley at the time. Yeah I see. Yeah, he was the bass player. I couldn't think of it. That's who, he had a Suzy part.
Well I hate to put words in your mouth, but John Porter used to talk to me about that. He kept a book everywhere.
Yeah, John Porter was living down on Simon Bollower and what you call him then at that time?
Oh Ryan Caliocco? Oh Ryan Caliocco.
Yeah, yeah. That's right. He had a good vision to me. Yeah, well he. About twelve ten or something like that.
Yeah, well he was there.
He was with me with this other band too. Yeah.
I still want to go back to that. If we got any more tape left. We got plenty. Yeah, you got plenty.
Yeah.
What about this neighborhood around Washington to Louisiana and LaSalle and Danielle and all the joints there? And you know, there were a lot of joints?

Well Chinatown was a joint. And Howard there, the Black Gold was a joint. And they had a rhythm club. It'd come up afterwards to the Italian boys that were driving in Jackson Avenue. They were over shore. Henry Harden was friends used to give them cocktail dances. Well they started to steal musicians, you know, from different bands. Joe got in debt with them people as usual. And he went back there, you know, and had all of them. Yeah, I think Russ was back there.
Yeah, Russ went back there.

And Buddy Charles, it was downstairs. Buddy Charles went back there with him too, playing guitar. When guitarists came out of the lake, we were on that guitar. He was playing back there, Buddy Charles was playing back there. It was Henry Harden's band. And Buddy Charles, Henry Harden, and one of his brothers there, John Casimir. William Casimir was playing with him. So actually the phone player that was?
Yeah, yeah.

You know his brother, the one player guitar died, Sam Casimir. When did he die? Oh, about three months ago somebody told me. He died in Chicago. And they was all playing back there with Henry Harden's band, at the rhythm club. Then afterwards he beat it, then Joe got in there. Joe had killed him.
Bucket and all that.
Show who? Show. What about Louisiana Avenue, was that a jumping place then?

No, well I played with a little trio over there at Robinson and Houston Avenue for a while there. Well I had oil on piano and I had a boy playing drums, I can't think of his name. You're on my lap, huh? Yeah I had oil on piano and I had another boy sing, play a great trumpet. No he sang, he played a drum. I got in with Celestan too when he went to Delco Island, I can't think of his name. But I know all those guys.
Well I'll call you later about it, I'll phone you up and you can phone me. Anyway, what about other streets like Jackson Avenue, is much happening there?

No, you see after the dewdrops started, Buddy Charles went in there with him and Mr. Kimball and a couple of more places, and the Robin Hood started, that was Paul Gaten, you understand? Paul Gaten started with a trio over there, you understand? And then things just as a standstill with, you know, those group combos, out of town attraction, nothing else happened. Well I was swinging with my band, everywhere. I was playing Creole Fiesta, you know, in different, out of the lake and down in Beerus, you understand? All those oranges grow all down in there. And then alternating in between the time I worked with Willie Pazio and Harold Dejon.
Was there much on St. Charles Avenue?

Well after I left, after I left Parisian Garden down there, I went up to St. Charles Avenue at Buckaroo Stadium in St. Charles, I went up there with this, well I told you, play clarinet, meet Charlie Hamilton and him and Brady.

Yeah, you told me before, I can't remember who, but anyway, what about Jewel's Tavern and Dixieland Inn or something, all those places, were there a lot of joints on St. Charles around the 1300 block there?

No, they used to have one at, Melchomene, St. Charles Minor, with, Minor, B Minor was playing up there with a group but they didn't have nothing compared with what we had. Now when I was playing at the cathedral at St. Charles, I had Ollie Popper playing bass, and you know, and Brady, that's the guy I couldn't think of at the time, had Ollie Popper playing bass. And we should call him, Charles Thomas was his name, we called him Ollie Popper. He was playing bass and Charlie Hamilton on piano and I was on guitar and Brady was on drums. And I used to sing that thing.
And what about Magazine Street and Chappatoulas, was there anything over that way in my childhood?

Well I used to work with Howard and them, sometimes after that job went under, with Abbie and Howard and Morgan, up at the line in Chappatoulas, and then later they built a place out near the river where I had left. Gee that's pretty near the river, Chappatoulas.
Yeah.

They built the front place out there. They got all the, oh you mean the patio? Yeah. Yeah, I used to go there and talk. This guy had a bar room there, I used to play there with Abbie and Howard in Malden. We used to play there on Sundays and different things. Then they built that other place out there where I had left then and I went on downtown, I started working with Boybanks and Al was what you call them.
What about Napoleon and Chappatoulas did you ever play that?
George Williams was playing out there. George Williams and somebody else. I don't know, I played out there one time with Bo Foster, somebody.
You know I think we'd better call it to a halt.

See a lot of them guys would hire you for a while, they wouldn't keep it because they were scared he was going to take the job, you know, when he could play. You understand what I mean? When he'd get in the jam, he'd have to hire you. But me I didn't make no difference who I had, as long as he could play. Always brought him out.
You weren't afraid of him?
No, couldn't play no more than I could. You see I still can play a little. Oh I know.
Well we thought, you wanted to ask something. Did you ever play with Punch Miller?

Yeah, Punch Miller. See Punch Miller left here long years ago and he come back here and I played a few jobs with him, and with him and Al Goodman the bass player, he's a little Al, and he's living down there on Full Street, and I played some jobs with him, but I didn't play too many but I played a good bit of them.
You never played out of time with him up on the road or something?

No, I don't know. I believe we went to, what the hell I went, I went to Pencil Court and Milton White and somebody, I know I went there with Andrew Anderson, and I went to Keith McPhee with George Williams, you know there's a naval bass player.
I was just getting everything out so you could sign the release and I couldn't pay you and stuff like that. Oh ok.
Well you're the boss. When you going to have another one in this session? Well I don't know.
You have to give us time to write this one up. What I mean do you like it?
Oh yeah.
I promised John L I'd interview him too, you know.
Oh yeah, John L, yeah. I think he'd like to do that.
Why don't we turn it off now and get the thing.
Ok, that's it. Yeah. Thank you. Thank you.
